utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the entire passage, or rather the third passage from the top on page 37 has to do with the issues I asked of the witness. In the middle of this particular paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you think you can favour the Bench and those of us who don't know B/C/S with the correct page of the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please, Your Honour. This is page 00362655, the last paragraph, which goes on to the next page, and I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have -- you say 00362655, Mr. Milovancevic, the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the third paragraph from the top on this page, which is page 37 in the B/C/S, commences with Mr. Kadijevic's assessment of what the representatives of the European Community's altitude toward the JNA was and their wish to have control over it, which we discussed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, after the point where he says that the activities aimed at having Mr. Mesic assume the position of the president of the Presidency with a view to -- I apologise -- with a view to assuming control over the army, which will make it impossible for the army to play any sort of independent role, or a role aimed at Serbian interests, there, Mr. Kadijevic says the following: "This phase ended quite soon because they, just as Mesic did, realised that no control could be established over the army. This was the case because of two reasons." Therefore, is it correct, Mr. Theunens, that Mr. Kadijevic in his book and the text that you quote here talks of two reasons why it was not possible for the European Community to control the army through Mesic, whereas you present these two reasons as the reasons for which purportedly General Kadijevic did not recognise Mesic? Are these two different things?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to bring us back to my report. The issue we were discussing was Stipe Mesic assuming the chairman of the SFRY Presidency as was normally intended to. All I tried to do is to focus on that. I didn't study the role of the international community in the conflict in 1991 prior to the deployment of UNPROFOR because then at least from analytical point of view, I wouldn't only use Kadijevic's book. I think the key issue in this section here is that indeed I used Kadijevic's book but I also looked at other sources and, in particular, JNA -- contemporaneous JNA documents from 1991, to find whether Kadijevic's views were corroborated or not whether it comes to the evolution of the mission of the JNA. Now, what Kadijevic alleges in relation to the responsibility or the role of the international community in the events in Croatia in 1991, I'm in no position whatsoever to comment or to discuss that because this is only one source. In analysis you don't work with just one source, you look at several sources. You look at the credibility, the reliability of the source, excuse me, the credibility of the information and you compare it and then you come to that assessment but it's not just one source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it controversial that Mr. Kadijevic says in this book that Mesic had no authority because he was trying to issue orders to the army through the media?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the passage on page 69 in the English version of my report tries to explain the attitude Kadijevic had towards Mesic. I think the paragraph there is quoted from Kadijevic's book is quite clear. Now, obviously there will be other passages in Kadijevic's book where he addresses his feelings towards Mr. Mesic but again that was outside the context of this report. In my opinion, the passage quoted on the top of page 69 is sufficient to understand the relation or - excuse me - the view Kadijevic as a Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command has on Stipe Mesic who was the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Are you aware of the fact that in February 1991, on the 20th of February 1991, the then Republic of Croatia decided to secede from Yugoslavia and took a decision to the effect that all of the -- all of Yugoslavia's laws ceased to have any validity on its territory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm aware of the overall developments at the time but I'm not aware of this specific decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that a referendum on the independence of Croatia and its secession from Yugoslavia was held in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware of a referendum for independence in Croatia in 1991, as I am also aware of similar referendums or referendum on the territory known as the SAO Krajina. Sorry, I have to add, with obviously other questions than the questions that were asked in the Croatian referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the previous page, page 68, did you not state that Stipe Mesic was elected or rather assumed the post of president of the Presidency at the intervention of the European Union? And that he assumed the role on the 1st of July, although the referendum for the secession of Croatia had already been held?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, referendum -- the referendum that was held in Croatia was not subject of my report, and in the context of the issue that was being discussed here, the overall command and control over the SFRY armed forces, I didn't consider that essential at that time. And I didn't consider it essential in that context, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the statement Mr. Mesic gave in late October 1991 upon leaving Belgrade and going to Croatia, to Zagreb? The statement read as follows: "I have accomplished my mission. Yugoslavia is no more."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard that statement quoted quite often but I don't recall exactly whether he really made it. I would have to see the statement, from my point of view, and when he made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that at the time when Mr. Mesic was appointed president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and he was a member from Croatia, he was a Croat, Ante Markovic was the federal Prime Minister, Budimir Loncar was foreign minister, both of them were Croats, head of the federal security services was also a Croat, Zdravko Mustac?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that Ante Markovic was the federal Prime Minister. The other people, I don't recall exactly what their duties were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These facts showing that the top offices of the state leadership of Yugoslavia were held by members of -- from a republic which was engaging in a secession, did you take them into account when analysing the reasons for the steps taken by the federal secretary of people's defence, General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not in a position to agree with the statement made by Mr. Milovancevic according to which allegedly all the top offices of the state leadership of Yugoslavia were being held by members of a republic which was engaging in a secession. I didn't analyse nor did I study the makeup of the various bodies of, be it political, military, at the SFRY level prior to summer 1991. It may well be correct. What I know for what the military is concerned that is that in particular after summer 1991, so from September 1991 onwards, the command positions, in particular for operational groups for the corps and related levels were all held by officers of Serbian or Montenegrin ethnicity. I have to add to that that many non-Serbs left or were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the parts of General Kadijevic's book, namely the text on page 38, which is on page 20 of the English version, where he says that there was an attempt of the European Community to assume control and influence over the JNA via Ante Markovic, federal Prime Minister, who was a Croat? [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we addressed this question a bit earlier. My report does not analyse the role of the European Community or other international actors in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia during the first half of 1991. In case I were to analyse this role, of course, I would look at Kadijevic's book but I would also look at publications or statements by representatives of the European Community at that time and other sources. I think it would be imprudent from an analytical point of view to draw conclusions only basing myself on one source, and at this stage I can only -- at this moment I can only look at one source. So I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to assess the military and political role of the JNA, as well as the acts of the military leadership, namely General Kadijevic, is it important to analyse political, military, and any other situation, including security situation, in the former Yugoslavia and in Croatia? Or did you analyse that situation solely through written material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are, I think, 300 references in the document, so in my report, 300 written sources that have been used and as we explained in the beginning of my examination, they can basically be categorised in four groups: We have legal documents, constitutions, laws, mainly SFRY and RSK. Secondly there are military documents from -- doctrinal documents, regulations, as well as situation reports, more specifically for latter half of 1991 and the events between 1992 and 1995, as well as orders from JNA officers, VJ, from JNA, VJ, SAO Krajina, RSK TO, as well as SVK. It is obvious -- and excuse me, to continue, next group of documents are open sources, most of the time open sources from SFRY origin. These documents were analysed with the goal of the report in view i.e., studying the establishment and the role of the SAO and RSK TO and SVK in the conflict in Croatia and the relation between these organisations and Milan Martic. I believe that in doing so, I did my utmost best to find the best compromise to a document that is complete but it is also still manageable. We have as I mentioned 300 references used. I do think that these references cover or assist me in achieving the goal I tried to achieve and, of course, it will be up to the Chamber to decide whether the goal has been achieved or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. On page 70 of your report, do you discuss that in early October 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY was reduced to the representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, Vojvodina, and Kosovo, and that, as such, it took a decision to declare the state of an imminent threat of war in October of 1991? Do you say that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and the references for this comments in the report can be found in the footnotes 208 and 209 which are Official Gazettes of the SFRY and later FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this came about and why was the SFRY Presidency reduced, as you termed it? How this came about?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't include that in my report, but I can refer to the diary of Borisav Jovic who describes in detail how, from summer 1991, various not only members of the Presidency but also people who are not part of the Presidency but at parallel meeting structures are being set up. He calls it the group of 6 and the group of 6 is for example mentioned in subparagraph 3 on page 69. I also remember that open sources report in great detail about the changes in the Presidency because some people don't attend any more or cannot attend or don't wish to attend, but again I didn't study the circumstances that led to this situation. I also wish to add that early October an amendment was adopted to the rules of procedure of the SFRY Presidency by a number of members of the SFRY Presidency, or maybe it could also have been adopted much earlier but anyway an amendment was adopted that allowed to take decisions with a smaller number of members present than used to be the case before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time, on the eve of October 1991, a representative of Slovenia, Mr. Denovsek, representative of Croatia, and the president, Mr. Mesic, representative of Macedonia, Mr. Tupurkovski, and the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Bogicevic all left the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is possible but I didn't study that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these four members of the Presidency, who left the Presidency, Mesic, Drnovsek, Tupurkovski, and Bogicevic were all representatives of the republics engaging in an unconstitutional secession from Yugoslavia, or simply republics engaging in secession from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will give the same answer. I'm not a political nor a legal expert. I didn't address these issues in my report so I cannot answer on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is clear that you're neither a political nor a legal expert, Mr. Theunens. I didn't claim anything otherwise, but I would like you to answer my question, which is: Such political changes, did they influence and were they able to influence the acts of the federal secretary of people's defence and other members of the Presidency, and if so, how could they influence them?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in reading Kadijevic's book, it is obvious that he has very strong views on what should be done, what could have been done. He expresses also very strong views on the attitude of a number of members of the Supreme Command, but I don't know to what extent Kadijevic's behaviour was influenced by certain events or not. I would also like to refer to the few excerpts I included of the book by Jovic because he gives the political side of the story. And based on what Jovic says especially from August 1991 onwards, there were many meetings between Jovic, Milosevic, political side, and on the other hand, Kadijevic and Adzic, which would indicate that the normal procedures whereby the military leadership carried out instructions given by the political leadership are more or less being applied even though it's not really the de jure political body that is giving these instructions to the military leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, would this be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this would be a good time for a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourns and reconvenes at half past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, may we just deal with housekeeping matters? It's just become to our notice that Friday the 3rd of February may be available to sit in Courtroom II in the morning. I thought I must find out from Mr. Milovancevic how much longer he thinks he will be with this witness. Should we take that day just in case we need it or shouldn't we? Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a very specific question and my answer will depend on the witness and his answers to my question. It is a bit difficult for me at this stage to assess the length of my cross-examination but I believe it should take three days in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, maybe it may be advisable to take the day, if everybody is available on that day. Would you be available, Mr. Milovancevic, on the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We would also be available, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everybody else, I would imagine. Okay, we will then book that day. That would be in Courtroom II, not in Courtroom III, and that will be at 9.00 in the morning. We will confirm that with the relevant people who are responsible for scheduling. Thank you very much. Coming back to your cross-examination, Mr. Milovancevic, looking at the transcript of the 26th of January, when the witness was being led by his counsel, he indicated that he dealt with a number of pages from this book that we have been talking about this morning, and it's not quite clear from the record whether the entire book was admitted into evidence because at some stage what the Bench said, it's indicated here that the microphone had not been activated, it seems safe to accept that only the pages that he referred to were admitted, because he says that, "I will start with the B/C/S version, it is between the ERNs" and he mentions them 000359489 and 00359499, and the English version corresponds with those pages. It doesn't seem as if the entire book was admitted. If you're going to be referring to other pages would you like to have those pages admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps the entire book should be admitted. Perhaps that's easier, to be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd have no objection to that, Your Honour. Hopefully we've specified the relevant portions from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well then, then the entire book is admitted and may it be given an exhibit number, the pages that were given an exhibit number, 24, maybe now the book may be given another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a suggestion? I think that the way it works in e-court is that the whole book was already in there and it's in such a way that it might be easier just to keep the same number but admit all pages. It's just a suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just asking myself. The book is on e-court, the whole book already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It seems to have the necessary numbers as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it does. Perhaps the Court officer can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I've just been corrected. The whole book is already into the evidence -- admitted into evidence as Exhibit number 24. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we left it off on page 80 or rather 70 of your report, paragraph 4, which deals with early October 1991, when, as you stated, the Presidency declared the state of an imminent threat of war on the territory of the SFRY as of the 1st October 1991. In your opinion, from a military point of view, were there any reasons in place for such a decision to be taken?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think actually it was the body that decides about this declaration of imminent threat of war that should be asked this question because I -- again I didn't analyse their motives, the reasons why they took the decision, so I cannot really comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the fact that some members of the Presidency had left the Presidency a bit earlier, one of the reasons for taking such a decision? Did it have any impact on the fact that this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness has just said that he didn't investigate the motives of the participants in the decision-making. How can he answer this question? It's the same question phrased differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with General Spegelj, Mr. Theunens? Do you know of the person?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm familiar with General Spegelj and his role in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How come you are familiar with his role when you stated that you did not study the role of the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are in my view two different things. It's not that because Martin Spegelj was a Croat and that he did certain things in the conflict I learned of while being involved in interviewing him as a witness for the Milosevic case, that this means that suddenly I have a view or I should have a view on what the Croatian side as such did. Spegelj was not the only Croat involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Spegelj a Minister of Defence in the Republic of Croatia in 1991? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, Your Honours, which duties he occupied in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he occupied any position in the armed forces of Croatia at all in 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he was involved in providing weapons to -- I'm not sure whether it was the ZNG or any other armed force of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In January 1991, did the SFRY Presidency take a decision to the effect that all those who had obtained weapons illegally be deprived of those weapons, the illegal formations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that's correct, and that applied to all the six constituting republics of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of March 1991, the special police forces of Croatia made an incursion into the police station in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Milovancevic is speaking about the municipality of Pakrac in Croatia. Now, again I haven't studied as I mentioned earlier, the role of the special police forces of Croatia or any other forces in Croatia, but I found the phrasing a bit particular that you speak about an incursion of a police force of Croatia into a police station on its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of March 1991, because of the events in Pakrac, did the JNA intervene? That was the reason why I put the earlier question, not just because of the Croatian special police force?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that the Croatian -- that the JNA intervened in the area even though, as I haven't studied the situation in Pakrac specifically, I cannot -- I'm not in a position to say why the JNA intervened and what the goal was of the JNA in intervention. And the reason I say that because I've written -- I read several accounts of the events in Pakrac and they don't always come to the same conclusions. So -- and this is also something actually I explained in the report, that initially, the official role of the JNA was represented as trying to separate the conflicting parties, most often these were on one hand Croatian police and on the other hand SAO Krajina or SAO Western Slavonia or the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem. Some have declared police forces with the latter, I mean Serbian self-declared police forces taking over certain police stations in a number certain of areas, the Croatian police wanting to re-establish Croatian authority, and then the JNA intervening to separate the parties. In a number of areas, like, for example, Borovo Selo which is outside the context of this report, because it -- Borovo Selo is located in Eastern Slavonia, volunteers from Serbia were involved in creating the incident or provoking the incident and the JNA intervention more or less consolidated the Serb control over these police stations on the territory of Croatia, I mean in Borovo Selo at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of March 1991, did the special police force fire upon the JNA in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen several accounts on the events in Pakrac. It may be reported in one of these accounts that the special police force of Croatia fired upon the JNA but I didn't analyse this incident so I'm not in a position to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact, Mr. Theunens, that between the 12th and the 15th of March 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY held a meeting at the suggestion of the -- of the Secretariat for National Defence with a proposal that a state of emergency be declared?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this meeting of the Presidency, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The suggestion coming from the top military leadership to the effect that a state of emergency be declared, was it in fact refused by the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that the request was refused but I don't know why it was refused because the question suggests that it was refused because it came from the top military leadership, and I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you've misunderstood my question, Mr. Theunens. And I'll repeat it to you, or you have distorted it. My question to you was the following: The proposal of the top military leadership for a state of emergency to be declared, was it refused? I didn't ask anything more or anything less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The answer was yes, it was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The proposal from the top military leadership for a state of emergency to be declared, does it also contain a statement that a civil war had already broken out in Yugoslavia, and did this not come only 12 days after the armed conflict in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that may well be possible but I don't recall the exact phrasing of the top military leadership proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of April, the Presidency session was on the 15th of March when the proposal for an emergency state was refused, that on the 1st of April, another conflict occurred in Plitvice between the Croatian police forces and the local Serb population?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to my recollection the events in Plitvice took place at the end of March 1991 but it also may be early April, and I'm not sure whether there was a conflict between Croatian police and the local Serb population or whether the conflict was between Croatian police and Serbian or let's say self-declared or members of a local Serb police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene in Plitvice in order to separate the two conflicting parties at the proposed -- at the request of the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I recall the JNA intervening. Now, I'm not 100 per cent sure of the outcome of the intervention, whether the intervention of course the two parties were separated but whether Croatian authority was restored over Plitvice, as it is located in Croatia, or whether actually the local Serb police stayed in power. I don't recall exactly the outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned this, but on the 2nd of May in Borovo, were there armed conflicts between on the one hand armed Serbs and on the other armed Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this conflict -- I mean, the incidents involved are not addressed in my report but I had to conduct research into these matters due to my work for the Seselj case here at the ICTY. There were indeed serious incidents on the 1st and 2nd of May in Borovo Selo between armed Serbs, both local Serbs as well as Serbs from Serbia who had gone to the area, as well as members of the police of the Republic of Croatia and not armed Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene in Borovo Selo to separate the two sides and thus in fact saved the Serbian -- the Croatian police officers?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, indeed the JNA intervened to separate the two sides but I don't know what effect that intervention had on the situation of the Croatian police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 25th of June, Slovenia and Croatia one-sidedly declared their -- unilaterally declared their independence from Yugoslavia, and you have to know that what happened on Borovo Selo was on the 1st and 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I misunderstood the question but the link between the events in Borovo Selo on one hand and the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia on the other hand is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will put a more specific question to you. I was merely trying to point out to the time difference of a bit over a month, that's to say that more than a month later, the declaration of Croatia's and Slovenia's independence took place. I did not want to point to any cause or link between the two so in fact did you know that on the 25th of June, Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, on the 25th of June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. After Slovenia declared its independence and took control over the -- of borders, did the JNA intervene in Slovenia immediately after?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, again this is not subject of my report but I know from the various sources, mainly open sources I consulted while working at ICTY, that indeed a number of JNA units intervened in Slovenia, even though it was not really clear what these JNA units tried to achieve and also indeed what the aim of this intervention was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, did you come across the decision of the federal executive council presided by Ante Markovic, to send 1.000 soldiers to Slovenia on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember seeing that decision. Again, because it's mainly also because it's outside the scope of my report, which focuses on SAO Krajina TO and RSK TO and SVK and the relationship between these armed organisations and Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your last answer, did you analyse in great detail day-to-day decisions of the top leadership concerning the engagement of the JNA and the change of its objectives, as you term them in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the executive summary and also from the start of this section, you see that based on the research I did and which was focused on the conflict in Croatia, this change in objective became most visible in summer 1991, so actually at the end of summer 1991 is after the event in Slovenia. That is why I didn't include the events in Slovenia, nor any decisions on the role of the JNA prior to summer 1991 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did armed conflicts break out in Slovenia in June, after the JNA managed to establish the authority of Yugoslavia along its borders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was indeed an armed conflict in Slovenia but as I've tried to explain earlier, these events are not the subject of my report, so it is hard for me to answer detailed questions about these particular events in Croatia -- in Slovenia, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. My question was merely whether armed conflicts broke out in Slovenia, nothing more. I hope we've understood each other. After the conflicts were concluded, did the Presidency of the SFRY adopt a decision to withdraw JNA forces from the territory of Slovenia in order to avoid any further clashes and victims?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- Your Honours, the SFRY Presidency indeed adopted such a decision. Now, to withdraw the JNA from the territory of Slovenia. There were probably several goals for that decision, and indeed coming back to the questions Mr. Milovancevic asked earlier, the outcome of the crisis in Slovenia could be seen as a first indicator in the change of the JNA's mission, based, of course -- I mean the change which was based or which was a result of the instructions given by the political leadership, the SFRY Presidency, and others, as I have mentioned, quoting from Jovic's book, so others involved in giving instructions and orders to the military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, after all of these events, the Presidency of the SFRY took a decision to declare a state of imminent threat of war on the 1st of October 1991. This is uncontested, is it, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is uncontested that the decision was taken on the 1st of October, but I am not aware of the exact reasons, the motives, why the reduced Presidency decided to declare a state of imminent threat of war on the territory of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Presidency of the SFRY, which adopted such a decision, had the necessary powers to do so?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is a legal question. All I've included in the report is the decision as such, as it was published. I mentioned also earlier during my cross-examination that at one moment in time, amendments were adopted, I'm not sure whether it was to the constitution or to the rules of procedure for the SFRY Presidency whereby the number of members that was required to take a decision was reduced and I also mentioned that the decision, based on the information I have, was taken by a reduced number of members of the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that you studied the rules of procedure of the Presidency, number of members, and voting procedure and so on. However, when I asked you about Mr. Mesic you claimed not to have read the rules and not to be familiar with these procedures. Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think my answers were both clear. First of all, and I repeat here, I didn't study the rules of procedure. However, when doing research on the decision of the -- on the decision of the declaration of the imminent state of war, I came across a document and I'm not sure whether it was an amendment to the rules of procedure or the constitution, according to which the number of members that were required to take a decision was reduced. I think there is a clear difference in these two answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given that you, as a military expert, are involved in studying international laws of war and international law, you have to have at least an elementary knowledge of the two. Are you familiar with the decision of the International Court of Justice which in essence recognises the right of federal authorities to -- regardless of the secession crisis, they assume their jurisdiction and their authorities in the entire territory of the country? This was the decision of the International Court of Justice pertaining to the South African union dated the 18th of July 1966, paragraph 32. This decision states that to invoke -- invoking the rights and protection of interests is something that only the holders of the title in the international law are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whether I'm a military expert or not, I think that's something Your Honours should decide, based on the report. Now, the other part of the question, it's really impossible for me to answer this because it's clearly a legal question which has no relation with my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, once again I don't want to interfere with your cross-examination but, you know, the way you have been asking questions, you can only get the kind of answer that you have just got now, and unfortunately you are not dealing with the issues that are before the Court. I'd just like to point that out to you, that right from the start of this case, I've just found you to be going just along the case and not on the case. I'm not quite sure what your defence is. I've surmised what I think your defence is from the way in which you conduct your defence but unfortunately, the way you have structured your defence makes you ask questions which most of the time I cannot see the relevance of. I just want to ask you to at least try to stay with the issues: Did Mr. Martic do the things that are alleged in the charges or didn't he do them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to say that the strategy of the Defence is affected by the strategy of the Prosecution which speaks of the joint criminal enterprise. In order to analyse the joint criminal enterprise, we have to delve into the issues covered by Mr. Theunens, namely the role of the Presidency, the role of the federal Secretariat of people's defence, the acts of all parties and armed forces. This is a very broad topic which covers numerous events, and sometimes it is very difficult to stick to specific facts, concrete facts, or those that are clearly visible and obvious. However, I will bear in mind your instructions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 71, Mr. Theunens, you state that the 14th corps withdrew to the area of Prijedor, Derventa, Zenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina while the 31st Corps withdrew to Serbia, after the JNA pulled out of Slovenia; is that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, and this comment is based on Exhibit 65 ter number 1223 which is a document from the SSNO dated 25th of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be shown on our screens Exhibit 1223, precisely the one mentioned by Mr. Theunens? Can this be put on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the Court officers are not able to find the document on the particulars you've given. Are you able to give an ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] B/C/S number is 00606845, 00606849. The English version is 00606850, 00606853. Your Honours, if it's difficult to find this document, we can come back to this later on, in order to avoid any further delay. I can continue with my questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, then. We'll continue and may the legal officers be trying to find it in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 71 of your report, Mr. Theunens, you state facts concerning the structure of the 5th military district, and you say, or rather this is what the chart shows, that the headquarters of the 5th military district was in Zagreb, that it covered the 10th corps, the 31st Corps, the 13th corps headquartered in Rijeka, another one headquarters in Varazdin, 329th Armoured Brigade, and another one headquartered in Ljubljana; is that correct, Mr. Theunens, that this is how you described it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these military units, large military units of the 5th military district and precisely the 31st Corps headquartered in Maribor and another one headquartered in Ljubljana, were they withdrawn from the territory of Slovenia in accordance with the decision that we have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can only talk about the document which is now visible on the screen, this order number 51-1 from the SSNO dated 25th of July 1991, according to which orders were given to withdraw the 31st Corps from mayor bore as well as to withdraw the 14th corps from Ljubljana so indeed these JNA units according to the order withdrew from Slovenia, even though if I remember well, the withdrawal operation took several weeks or even months to be finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on the book of Mr. Kadijevic, my view of the break-up, do you remember that he spoke of the fact that the formations of the JNA which were withdrawing from Slovenia pursuant to the order of the Presidency of the SFRY were attacked during their withdrawal and their weapons seized in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have to see the page in the book of Kadijevic. I recall that he writes about it but I don't recall the exact details of what -- of the events Kadijevic describes, and to what extent weapons were seized, all the weapons, some weapons. It's a very broad statement which is basically impossible to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer is quite sufficient. Thank you, Mr. Theunens. In this chart shown on page 71, at the top of the chart, you say that the 5th military district was headquartered erred in Zagreb and that following August 1991, it was partially deployed to Slunj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, because at the latest at the end of August, Croatians started to block or erect barricades in the vicinity of JNA barracks and garrisons, and a number of barracks and garrisons were therefore prematurely withdrawn or others were withdrawn later on after negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fate of the 32nd Varazdin corps mentioned on this chart of the 5th military corps? It was commanded by General Vlado Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know from my work here that the situation of the 32nd Corps in Varazdin was very difficult because the barracks were blocked and I wouldn't use the expression besieged but I will just summarise the situation there was very difficult, and that the General Trifunovic at one moment decided to surrender. His decision to surrender was taken very badly in -- by his superiors in the JNA and therefore at a later stage a trial against General Trifunovic took place, and I think recently or a few years ago, Trifunovic was -- or the proceedings against Trifunovic were dropped and he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who blocked the barracks of the 32nd Corps headquartered in Varazdin? Which forces did that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours I use the expression Croatians because I'm not sure which forces were involved and to what extent also maybe civilian population was involved but it could have been ZNG, Croatian police, maybe some civilians, maybe some volunteers. Again, I haven't studied the blockade of the JNA barracks in Varazdin in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens, that's sufficient. Are you familiar with the fact given by General Spegelj that by taking the 32nd Corps of the JNA in Varazdin, a large amount of weaponry was confiscated as well, tanks, armoured vehicles, ammunition, cannons and so on, and also a large amount of equipment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not familiar with Spegelj -- with General Spegelj's specific comment on the takeover of the barracks of the 32nd Corps in Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that by taking the facilities of the 32nd Corps of the JNA in Varazdin, or rather that this took place in September or in the second half of September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the blockades of barracks in Croatia became -- I won't use the expression generalised but it became part of a more concerted effort from the Croatian side from the end of August 1991 onwards. Still, I don't recall exactly when the barracks of Varazdin -- when the blockade there started, and when Trifunovic surrendered the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that the 265th Mechanised Armoured Brigade of the JNA in Bjelovar also fell into the hands of somebody else in the second half of September 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, Your Honours. As I mentioned from the end of August onwards, several JNA barracks and garrisons in -- on -- in Croatia were blocked by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the barracks in Bjelovar because, at the time, a huge amount of weaponry was also seized, tanks, trucks, over 100 trucks, over many tonnes of ammunition and so on. Did you hear of this information, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't hear about the barracks in Bjelovar specifically but it's obvious that when a barracks were surrendered or taken over otherwise, that there is a distinct possibility to acquire for those who take the barracks as a distinct possibility to obtain weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment, even though there are clear regulations within all armed forces to destroy all equipment when there is a risk that it may fall or that it will fall in the hands of the enemy. I remember that in that time period, General Adzic issued an order to prevent military equipment, JNA equipment, from falling into the hands of the Croats and gave instructions, gave orders for the destruction of such equipment, but I'm not sure whether I included it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the losses of the JNA in terms of military equipment, ammunition, and weapons? Do you know anything even roughly about their losses during that period of time, September through December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when mentioning September through December 1991 that is actually the time period when the armed conflict in the disputed areas or the disputed parts of Croatia becomes generalised so ammunition will be used, military equipment will be used, there will be losses, of course; I mean, it's unavoidable. There were indeed cases where Croats who besieged barracks took over equipment and ammunition. There are also examples of JNA units handing over equipment and ammunition to local Serbs. So the word "losses" covers several aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you judged the acts of the JNA and its military leadership in 1991, given the situation, did you also take into account the fact that Croatian forces seized about 200.000 automatic rifles of -- and other small arms, 500 tonnes of ammunition of all calibres, 500 tonnes of antitank mines, 2.000 tonnes of antipersonnel mines, about 240 tanks and 320 armoured personnel carriers? Did you take this information into account and are you familiar with this information at all?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't judge anyone in my report because, first of all, it's not my task. Secondly, I described the role of certain groups, organisations and individuals, I don't think that there are any judgements included. Now, secondly, I would have to see, when it comes to the figures you have listed, Mr. Milovancevic, I have to -- I would have to see the document. Now, at first glance, the amounts seem quite significant because -- I mean, I come from tanks. Like, 240 tanks, I don't doubt it, but for me it seems like a huge number because it's more than the Belgian armed forces. Of course, the Belgian armed forces are not relevant in this context but it's a -- quite a huge amount. I would say that without wanting to drag it on, but if Croatia had this equipment and the personnel to use the equipment, I think that the outcome of the conflict in 1991 would have been significantly different. But, again, I haven't -- I don't have your source in front of me so I would have to look at that and also look at other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you please just try to confine yourself to the answering the question? What you have said is of very great political interest, but not absolutely on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The data I just gave you, Mr. Theunens, is the data coming from Mr. Spegelj, the Minister of Defence of Croatia. This information was publicly available. We can now turn to the next section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Milovancevic, that the witness indicated that he hadn't studied Croatia and the military personnels of Croatia in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour. I'm not asking the witness anything about the Croatian armed forces and personnel. All I'm trying is to put to him the losses of the JNA in the territory of Croatia at the time when it was a regular legal armed force in its own territory, attacked by illegal armed formations. I am putting these questions because I believe that in order to assess the acts of the JNA, the state leadership and the military leadership, one had to consider very relevant the situation on the ground. I believe that it was of utmost importance. I also think that this assessment cannot be made only on the basis of papers, meaning various orders, instructions and so on. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on page 72, under item 3, which is entitled, "Evolution of the mission of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia," you discuss these matters precisely. In doing so, you quote the words of army General Veljko Kadijevic or rather his point of view that he presented in his book, "My view of the break-up," is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Kadijevic's book is one of the sources I consulted to describe this evolution. When you look further down in the report, on -- from page 76 onwards, I also quote from other sources and they may well statements by Kadijevic but those were then statements he made when he was still federal Secretary for People's Defence. I've also included orders or statements from General Adzic, like on page 78, and again another order by Kadijevic on the page 80, together with the book by Borisav Jovic or certain excerpts of that book we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that Mr. Kadijevic in his book explains the mission and the objectives of the armed forces of the SFRY during the conflict in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kadijevic, in -- or General Kadijevic in his book gives his analysis of the evolution or what he calls the evolution, I think he even used the expression"radical change" -- "radically changed mission" and what I tried to do is to compare that source. So Kadijevic's book which was published in 1993 with the evolution on the ground, evolution on the ground for which I have used orders and statements I just quoted, so orders and statements made in 1991. I've also compared the situation as it existed on the 23rd of November 1991, when a cease-fire agreement was signed in Geneva between Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Milosevic and General Kadijevic, compared all these sources and reports with the book of Kadijevic and I tried to summarise that in this part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the issue of the role of the armed forces, or rather the role and the objectives of the SFRY during the conflict in Yugoslavia, do you, as a military expert, distinguish between what is the constitutional definition of the role of the armed forces and the specific war objectives and tasks, including political objectives, that are determined and defined for any army?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. In a sense, I didn't compare them as such to come to a -- I will rephrase that. What I did was I listed first the constitutional mission, as it has been listed in section 1, and then, as I explained, I consulted various sources, the ones that I discussed between page 72 and page 80, and, okay, I came to a conclusion which basically reflected the sources mentioned between page 72 and page 80, and this conclusion -- according to this conclusion the goal of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia changed, at the latest in summer 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please show page 93 in B/C/S and page 60 in the English of Exhibit 24 on our screens? While this is being done, does Mr. Kadijevic in his book say that in his opinion, in March of 1991, the best option for the JNA was to rely on those political forces in the federation and those nations which wished to continue living in Yugoslavia while peacefully parting with those who wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. That's indeed what Kadijevic says but I believe in the English translation it's on page 61, so on the next page. Page 61 of his book. It is more or less in the middle of this third paragraph. More or less the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this political and military assessment, in your opinion, require a change in the missions and tasks of the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question but I would say if you agree with the peaceful parting as Kadijevic mentions it on this page then, of course, the mission would be adjusted but that would be a result of negotiations and talks between all the peoples of a peaceful solution. Now, if you choose for a military way to achieve or implement this goal, then again, yeah, that would, of course, have implications for the constitutional goal of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you not -- did you say a while ago that Croatia opted for the military option, blocked JNA barracks, attack them, and engaged in open military conflict?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are a lot of developments in 1991. Page 61 of Kadijevic's book refers to the situation in March 1991, before Pakrac, before Plitvice, examples Mr. Milovancevic mentions, and the blockade of the barracks happens a number of months later. It becomes more organised, end of August, course of September 1991. And it is also what is shown in the report at the -- the change in the mission becomes most visible after summer 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at paragraph 2 on page 93 of the text that's before you, where Mr. Kadijevic talks of the third stage. Could you please read the entire paragraph from that point on for us?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean page 93 of the English version or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's in the B/C/S, page 93.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Page 60.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we now on page 60 on the e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. I apologise. I have page 93 before me. That's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you have found the page, can you just let us know so that we can be on the same page, literally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's page 49 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out for us the second paragraph from the top, the third stage or phase commences up to the end of the paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again? How does the paragraph start in English? Is it in its attitude towards Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague told me that this was the last paragraph on page 49. I apologise. In the B/C/S it's the first paragraph whereas in the English version, it's the last paragraph. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe the paragraph begins, "The third phase began when Germany," and continues from there, but I also note that we are about to run over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the text for us, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honours. "The third phase began when Germany acting through the European Community openly took over management of the Yugoslav crisis, compelled Slovenia and Croatia to accelerate their secession by having them apply force, while at the same time preparing the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina with a double aim: To make the final fall of Yugoslavia so violent and brutal that it would never return to the stage of history again, and to provide a good excuse for striking a political and military blow against Serbia in order to defeat and humiliate it, cut it down to the size of a Belgrade pashadom and teach it a lesson once and for all. At the beginning of this phase, the armed forces task radically changed and was to, first, defend the Serb nation in Croatia and its national interest; two, pull JNA garrisons out of Croatia; three, gain full control of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the ultimate aim of defending the Serb nation and its national rights when the issue arose; four, create and defend the new Yugoslav state of those Yugoslav nations that desire to be part of it, meaning in this phase the Serb and Montenegrin nations, the basic conflict -- the basic concept for deployment of the armed forces was thus adjusted to this modified task."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before you go on, what does pashadom mean? There is a reference to a Belgrade pashadom, what does it mean, from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there must be a historical explanation for the word pashadom but I'm not aware of that one. But I assume Kadijevic means that in his view, Germany wants to reduce Serbia to a kind of mini state around Belgrade. According to Kadijevic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the time, Your Honour, I would wish to put a short question to the witness and then we could adjourn for the day. I believe that was the schedule, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The armed actions taken by Croatia in the process of secession, did they affect the conduct and acts of the JNA and the SFRY leadership in this period?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, this is a very complicated question. All I can say is that a conflict, an armed conflict always involves two parties, and the behaviour of each party has an impact on the behaviour of the other party. It's like action and reaction. Now, to what extent this theoretical description I just gave applies to the situation in Croatia, I think a detailed analysis of the events between -- I would even say 1980 and 1990 would be necessary in order to -- and 1991, would be necessary in order to be able to provide an answer to that question. It's not as simple as Mr. Milovancevic tried to put it here, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all for today, Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Court adjourns to tomorrow at 9.00, same court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of January, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
